entry.title: Assignment 1
entry.content:
Instructions

  • Read chapter 1 and sections 2.1 and 2.2 in Mathematics in Lean

  • Do the exercises below, by replacing each sorry with tactics.

  • Do the following exercises:

    • LeanCourse/MIL/C02_Basics/S01_Calculating.lean
    • LeanCourse/MIL/C02_Basics/S02_Proving_Identities_in_Algebraic_Structures.lean

    There are solutions in the solution folder in case you get stuck.

Note that the exercises only make sense while reading the chapter at the same time, so make sure you open mathematics in Lean in a browser.

My Solutions

See assignment 1 of my fork of the course. Here are some notes that I made while solving assigment 1.

Here I try to prove the same thing using rw tactic but from the other side.


example (a b c d : ℝ) (h : b = d + d) (h' : a = b + c) : a + b = c + 4 * d := by {
  calc a + b = b + c + b := by congr; 
      _      = 2*b + c   := by ring
      _      = 2*(d + d) + c := by congr; 
      _      = 4*d + c       := by ring 
      _      = c + 4*d       := by ring 
  }

/- ## Rewriting with a lemma

In the previous examples, we rewrote the goal using a local assumption. But we can
also use lemmas. For instance let us prove a lemma about exponentiation.
Since `ring` only knows how to prove things from the axioms of rings,
it doesn't know how to work with exponentiation.
For the following lemma, we will rewrite with the lemma
`exp_add x y` twice, which is a proof that `exp(x+y) = exp(x) * exp(y)`.
-/
-- In this example we start by identifying the LHS of exp_add in the goal
-- and simplifying
example (a b c : ℝ) : exp (a + b + c) = exp a * exp b * exp c := by {
  rw [exp_add (a + b) c]
  rw [exp_add a b]
  }

-- Alternatively, we can also start by simplifying the RHS 
example (a b c : ℝ ) : exp (a + b +c) = exp a * exp b * exp c := by {
   -- The RHS is already in the for (exp a * exp b) * exp c 
   rw [<- exp_add a b]  -- matches against (exp a * exp b) and re-writes it to exp (a+b)
   rw [<- exp_add (a+b) c] 
}

If we don't provide arguments to the lemmas, Lean will rewrite the first matching subexpression. I will in general try to avoid this as I am still learning, so the goal is to be as explicit as possible, even if that means a longer proof.

entry.title: Lecture 1
entry.content:
We start off with some Lean-specific definitions.

(Proposition)

A proposition (Prop) is a statement that is either true or false.

(Predicate)

A predicate is a function that takes arguments and returns a Prop.

Example:

/-- The sequence `u` of real numbers converges to `l`. -/
def SequenceHasLimit (u : ℕ → ℝ) (l : ℝ) : Prop :=
  ∀ ε > 0, ∃ N : ℕ, ∀ n ≥ N, |u n - l| < ε

For example, SequenceHasLimit is a predicate of type (ℕ → ℝ) → ℝ → Prop.

Partially applying it, SequenceHasLimit u is of type ℝ → Prop — it takes a real number l and returns the proposition that u converges to l.

Only when all arguments are supplied do we get a Prop. That is, SequenceHasLimit u x₀ is a Prop — it is the statement that the sequence u converges to x₀, defined as:

$$\forall \varepsilon > 0, \exists N \in \mathbb{N}, \forall n \geq N, |u_n - x_0| < \varepsilon$$

This statement may or may not have a proof, but it is a well-formed proposition.

A Note: Curried Functions

In Lean (and in type theory generally), multi-argument functions are curried by default, not tupled. So:

#check (add_complex_i : ℂ → ℂ)

def less_than_pi (x : ℝ) : Prop := x < π

#check less_than_pi
-- ⊢ ℝ → Prop


def less_than (x y : ℝ) : Prop :=
  x < y

-- ℝ → (ℝ → Prop)
#check (less_than)

The difference between these two signatures is:

  • ℝ → ℝ → Prop (curried) — takes one ℝ, returns a function ℝ → Prop. This is what Lean uses.

First Proof

Now let us look at a slightly non-trivial first proof in Lean. We start off by defining what it means for a sequence to have a limit, and for a function to be continuous.

/-- The sequence `u` of real numbers converges to `l`. -/
def SequenceHasLimit (u : ℕ → ℝ) (l : ℝ) : Prop :=
  ∀ ε > 0, ∃ N : ℕ, ∀ n ≥ N, |u n - l| < ε

/-- The function `f : ℝ → ℝ` is continuous at `x₀`. -/
def ContinuousAtPoint (f : ℝ → ℝ) (x₀ : ℝ) : Prop :=
  ∀ ε > 0, ∃ δ > 0, ∀ x, |x - x₀| < δ →
  |f (x) - f (x₀)| < ε

Then we state our first lemma:

If a sequence $u: \mathbb{N} \rightarrow \mathbb{R}$ converges to $x_0$, and a function $f: \mathbb{R} \rightarrow \mathbb{R}$ is continuous at $x_0$, then the sequence $f(u(n))$ converges to $f(x_0)$.

We first prove this theorem on "paper" like we are used to, but in a way that is directly (or almost directly) translatable to Lean. This will give us a mental model of how to think of proofs in Lean. The unfold commands just expand out the goals for better viewing.

Proof.

For the sequence to converge we need $$\forall \varepsilon > 0, \exists N \in \mathbb{N}, \forall n \geq N, |f(u(n)) - f(x_0)| < \varepsilon$$

This is our GOAL. The steps of the proof are as follows.

  1. Let $\varepsilon > 0$ be arbitrary. [Line 7]
  2. As $f$ is continuous at $x_0$, we get a $\delta > 0$ such that $\forall x, |x - x_0| < \delta \implies |f(x) - f(x_0)| < \varepsilon$. [Line 12] uses $\varepsilon$ above for the definition of continuity (works as it's greater than 0), and stores as f_prop the proposition $\forall x \in \mathbb{R}, |x - x_0| < \delta \implies |f(x) - f(x_0)| < \varepsilon$.
  3. As $u$ converges to $x_0$, we obtain $N$ by passing $\delta > 0$ as the value for $\varepsilon$ in the definition. We denote with u_prop the proposition that for all $n \geq N$, we have $|u(n) - x_0| < \delta$. [Line 17]
  4. We pick this $N$ to be the $N$ in our goal. [Line 19]
  5. Let $m \ge N$ be arbitrary [Line 21]. Now hn stores the proposition that $|u(m) - x_0| < \delta$ (after specialising to use the $m$ we introduced) [Line 22].
  6. Specialise f_prop with u_prop i.e. $x = u(m)$. As $|u(m) - x_0| < \delta$, we get $|f(u(m)) - f(x_0)| < \varepsilon$.
▢
 1lemma first_proof (f : ℝ → ℝ) (u : ℕ → ℝ) (x₀ : ℝ)
 2    (u_lim : SequenceHasLimit u x₀)
 3    (f_cont : ContinuousAtPoint f x₀) :
 4    SequenceHasLimit (f ∘ u) (f x₀) := by {
 5  unfold SequenceHasLimit
 6  -- Let ε > 0 be arbitrary
 7  intro (ε : ℝ) (hε : ε > 0)
 8  -- Since `f` is continuous, we can pick a `δ > 0` such that
 9  -- for all `x`, `|x - x₀| < δ → |f(x) - f(x₀)| < ε`.
10  unfold ContinuousAtPoint at f_cont
11  -- We want to invoke f_cont with eps and by assumption
12  obtain ⟨δ, hδ, f_prop⟩ := f_cont ε (by exact hε )
13  -- obtain ⟨δ, hδ, f_prop⟩ := f_cont ε (by assumption) -- also works if we don't want to remember hε 
14  -- Since `u` converges to `x₀`, we can pick a `N` such that
15  -- for all `n ≥ N`, `|u_n - x₀| < δ`.
16  unfold SequenceHasLimit at u_lim 
17  obtain ⟨N, u_prop⟩ := u_lim δ hδ
18  -- We pick this `N` to show that `f ∘ u` has limit `f(x₀)`.
19  use N
20  -- If `n ≥ N` we have `|u_n - x₀| < δ`,
21  intro m hn
22  specialize u_prop m hn
23  -- hence `|f(u_m) - f(x₀)| < ε`.
24  specialize f_prop (u m) u_prop
25  -- This finishes the proof.
26  exact f_prop  
27  }

Some comments:

obtain ⟨δ, hδ, f_prop⟩ := f_cont ε hε

or if you wanted to be maximally explicit with by:

have hε' : ε > 0 := by exact hε
obtain ⟨δ, hδ, f_prop⟩ := f_cont ε hε'

The (by assumption) on Line 13 is just finding hε : ε > 0 from the context automatically. Since you already have hε in scope, you can pass it directly as a term — no tactic needed at all. The by assumption version is a convenience for when you don't want to remember/type the exact hypothesis name.

The Re Write Tactic

example (a b c d : ℝ) (h : a + b = c - d) : 2 * (a + b) = 2 * c - 2 * d := by {
  rw [h, mul_sub]
  }

The rw tactic takes a list of rewrite rules and applies them left to right, in sequence. So rw [h, mul_sub] does two rewrites:

h — rewrites a + b to c - d, transforming the goal from 2 * (a + b) = 2 * c - 2 * d to 2 * (c - d) = 2 * c - 2 * d mul_sub — this is a Mathlib lemma stating a * (b - c) = a * b - a * c. It rewrites 2 * (c - d) to 2 * c - 2 * d, making the goal 2 * c - 2 * d = 2 * c - 2 * d, which closes automatically by reflexivity. Alternatively,

example (a b c d : ℝ) (h : a + b = c - d) : 2 * (a + b) = 2 * c - 2 * d := by {
  rw [h]
  rw [mul_sub]
}

also works.

The Ring Tactic

Basic properties of addition, subtraction and multiplication that are supported by rings are handled by the ring tactic.

example (a b c d : ℝ) (h : a + b = c - d) : 2 * (a + b) = 2 * c - 2 * d := by {
  rw [h]
  ring 
}

This also works instead of re-writing mul_sub.

The Congr + Calc Tactic

The congr tactic is an attempt to prove LHS = RHS, and if this fails, it changes the goal to a sub-goal of proving the bit that does. The way it works is best illustrated with an example: Say the goal is

⊢ f (g (x + y)) = f (g (y + x))

Writing congr, Lean sees that the LHS and RHS both have f( ) = f( ), so it first reduces the goal to proving g(x+y) = g(y+x). Then it trying to prove equality again, and finds that both sides have g( ) = g( ), so the new goal is x+y = y+x. Then it tries to prove equality again, and sees that if we proved x=y and y=x we would be done. The command congr x applies the tactic x times. So when the goal is

⊢ f (g (x + y)) = f (g (y + x))

  1. congr 1: would make the goal g(x+y) = g(y+x)
  2. congr 2: would make the goal (x + y) = (y+x)
  3. congr 3 or highher would result in two cases x=y and y=x.
example (a b : ℝ) (f g : ℝ → ℝ) : f (g (a + b) ) = f (g (b + a)) := by
  congr 2 -- try increasing it to see the issue.
  ring

The calc tactic allows us to string together many congr and ring tactics. As shown below:

example (a b c d : ℝ) (h : c = b*a - d) (h' : d = a*b) : c = 0 := by
  calc
    c = b*a - d   := by congr
    _ = b*a - a*b := by congr
    _ = 0         := by ring

congr is cleve about using the hypotheses to figure out the expansions for c and d. Alternatively we can also use the hypotheses directly:

-- Alternate view
example (a b c d : ℝ) (h : c = b*a - d) (h' : d = a*b) : c = 0 := by
  calc
    c = b*a - d   := by exact h
    _ = b*a - a*b := by rw [h']
    _ = 0         := by ring

exact tells Lean to expand c using the h rule exactly. rw [h] replaces the LHS of h with the RHS. NOTE: rw [<- h'] will replace the RHS with LHS.

The gcongr tactic generalises congr tactic to inequalities

example (a b : ℝ) (h : b ≤ a) : a + b ≤ 2*a := by
  calc
    a + b ≤ a + a := by gcongr
    _  = 2*a := by ring

Simp

Next tactic we have in computation is the simplifier simp. It will repeatedly apply a number of lemmas that are marked as simplification lemmas. For instance the proof below simplifies x - x to 0 and then |0| to 0.

Intro + Apply

The apply tactic can be used to specialize universally quantified statements.

example (f : ℝ → ℝ) (hf : even_fun f) : f (-3) = f 3 := by
  apply hf 3

/-
Fortunately, Lean is willing to work for us, so we can leave out the `3` and
let the `apply` tactic compare the goal with the assumption
and decide to specialize it to `x = 3`.
-/

example (f : ℝ → ℝ) (hf : even_fun f) : f (-3) = f 3 := by
  apply hf

/-
In the following exercise, you get to choose whether you want help from Lean
or do all the work.
-/
example (f : ℝ → ℝ) (hf : even_fun f) : f (-5) = f 5 := by
  apply hf (5)

When i want to prove something like for all $x \in X$, $f(x)$ is true, i use the intro tactic. The intro tactic is akin to when we write in a real proof, let $x$ be an arbitrary element of set $X$, and then we prove that $f(x)$ is true.

example (f g : ℝ → ℝ) (hf : even_fun f) : even_fun (g ∘ f) := by
  unfold even_fun
  intro x
  specialize hf x
  calc
    (g ∘ f) (-x) = g (f (-x)) := by simp
    _            = g (f x) := by rw [hf]
    _            = (g ∘ f) (x) := by simp

In the above example we introduce $x$ and then specialise the hf function at x.

Alternate proof using apply

example (f g : ℝ → ℝ) (hf : even_fun f) : even_fun (g ∘ f) := by
  intro x
  calc
    (g ∘ f) (-x) = g (f (-x))   := by simp
    _            = g (f x)      := by congr 1; apply hf

A note about how apply works

apply H : H must be a hypothesis or theorem with type P1 -> P2 -> ... -> PN -> Q, where the goal has type Q. This tactic will replace the goal with N separate goals, P1, through PN, as it corresponds to deciding to prove the premises of H and then using it to prove the goal. In the simply case where you just have P -> Q this will replace Q with P.

In the above example, after congr 1, we had to prove f (-x) = f x, so why did apply hf work when hf: even_fun f? The reason for this is for any predicate P

∀ x, P x is definitionally (x : ℝ) → P x in Lean's type theory. So apply on a universally quantified hypothesis works exactly like the P → Q pattern — the "premise" is just the implicit argument that Lean resolves automatically.

even_fun f unfolds to ∀ x, f (-x) = f x, which in Lean's type theory is:

hf : (x : ℝ) → f (-x) = f x

So when I did apply hf, Lean then asked for an intro x which we had.

  • P (premise): (x : ℝ) — you need to provide a real number
  • Q (conclusion): f (-x) = f x — you get a proof of equality for that number. And as I did intro x I had a proof for that number.

This is how we say the apply tactic allows us to specialise. Alternatively, I could have specialised h earlier, and not needed to use hf.

def non_decreasing (f : ℝ → ℝ) := ∀ x₁ x₂, x₁ ≤ x₂ → f x₁ ≤ f x₂
example (f : ℝ → ℝ) (hf : non_decreasing f) (x₁ x₂ : ℝ) (hx : x₁ ≤ x₂) : f x₁ ≤ f x₂ := by
  apply hf x₁ x₂ hx

Here as hf is telling us that f is non_decreasing, so when we apply hf with the argumeents x1, x2 and the hypothesis that x1 <= x2, we reduce to getting what we need.

R cases

In order to use h : ∃ x, P x, we use the rcases tactic to fix one x₀ that works.

example (a b c : ℤ) (h₁ : a ∣ b) (h₂ : b ∣ c) : a ∣ c := by
  rcases h₁ with ⟨k, hk⟩ -- we fix some `k` such that `b = a * k` i.e. hk: b = a * k
  rcases h₂ with ⟨l, hl⟩ -- we fix some `l` such that `c = b * l` i.e. hl: c = b * l
  -- Since `a ∣ c` means `∃ k, c = a*k`, we need the `use` tactic.
  use k*l
  calc
    c = b*l     := by congr
    _ = (a*k)*l := by congr
    _ = a*(k*l) := by ring

Complex Applies with specialise

-- You don't need to specialise but this is more exolicit
example (f g : ℝ → ℝ) (hf : non_decreasing f) (hg : non_increasing g) :
    non_increasing (g ∘ f) := by
  unfold non_increasing at *
  unfold non_decreasing at *
  intro x1 x2 hx
  specialize hf x1 x2
  specialize hg (f (x1)) (f (x2))
  apply hg
  apply hf
  exact hx

entry.title: Lecture 2
entry.content:
fun x : ℝ ↦ x ^ 2 Read it as: "the function that takes x (a real number) and maps it to x²"

fun — introduces an anonymous function (like λ) x : ℝ — the parameter x of type real ↦ — "maps to" (the Lean 4 symbol for => in lambda expressions) x ^ 2 — the body/output

Forward Reasoning : Have

One uses the have tactic, which introduces a new hypothesis. We read have new hypothesis h by apply hq hp.

apply H : H must be a hypothesis or theorem with type P1 -> P2 -> ... -> PN -> Q, where the goal has type Q. This tactic will replace the goal with N separate goals, P1, through PN, as it corresponds to deciding to prove the premises of H and then using it to prove the goal. In the simply case where you just have P -> Q this will replace Q with P.

Since hq : p → q, the goal of is a function expecting a proof of p, and hp : p is exactly that, applying hq to hp produces a proof of q which is my new hypothesis h. In other words, apply reduces the task of finding a proof of q to finding a proof for p, as I have a proof for p, I immediately "have" a proof h for q.

We will start with reasoning with implications in Lean.
-/

/-
**Forwards Reasoning** is reasoning forwards from the hypotheses that other facts must hold.
We can do this with the `have` tactic.
`intro` is used to introduce assumptions.
`exact` or `assumption` can be used to finish the proof.
-/

example (p q r : Prop) (hq : p → q) (hr : p → q → r) : p → r := by {
  intro (hp: p) -- Assume I have p 
  have h := by apply hq hp -- (h:q)
  have h' := by apply hr hp h  -- (h': q->r) at first and then (h': r) 
  exact h'
  }

Forward reasoning starts from what you already know (your hypotheses) and builds towards the goal.

Instead of naming new hypotheses, I can just specialise the existing ones.


/- We can also use `specialize` to apply a hypothesis to arguments. -/
example (p q r : Prop) (hq : p → q) (hr : p → q → r) : p → r := by {
  intro (hp: p) -- Assume I have p 
  specialize hq hp -- I specialise (hq: p->q) to (hq: q) because i give it p 
  specialize hr hp  -- I specialise (hr: p -> q-> r) to (hr: q-> r) because i get it p
  specialize hr hq  -- I specialise (hr: r) to r because i give it q
  exact hr 
}

Backwards Reasoning

Backward reasoning starts from what you need to prove (the goal) and works back towards your hypotheses. You say: "I need s. It suffices to prove r (because hrs : r → s). It suffices to prove q (because hqr : q → r). It suffices to prove p — which I already have." I reduce my goal to p whereas previously, I started with p and found a way to get to the goal.

-- Here we work backwards
example (p q r s : Prop) (hpq : p → q) (hqr : q → r) (hrs : r → s) : p → s := by {
  intro hp
  -- "To prove s, it suffices to prove r" (refine hrs ?_)
  refine hrs ?_
  -- goal: r
  -- "To prove r, it suffices to prove q" (refine hqr ?_)
  refine hqr ?_
  -- goal: q
  -- "To prove q, it suffices to prove p" (refine hpq ?_)
  refine hpq ?_
  -- goal: p
  exact hp
}

Using Lemmas

-- At each line I asked apply?
example : Continuous (fun x ↦ 2 + x * Real.sin x) := by {
  -- Get two cases Continous f and 
  -- Contnous g
  apply Continuous.add  
  . exact continuous_const
  . refine Continuous.mul ?hg.hf ?hg.hg --
    . exact continuous_id 
    . exact continuous_sin
  }

Linarith


example (h₀ : a = b) (h₁ : b < c) (h₂ : c ≤ d) (h₃ : d < e) : a < e := by
  calc a
      = b := h₀
    _ < c := h₁
    _ ≤ d := h₂
    _ < e := h₃

/- `linarith` can prove inequalities (and equalities)
  that follow from linear combinations of assumptions. -/

example (h₀ : a = b) (h₁ : b < c) (h₂ : c ≤ d) (h₃ : d < e) : a < e := by {
  linarith
  }

Universal Quantifies

The tactics for universal quantification and implication are the same.

  • We can use intro to prove an universal quantification (or implication).
  • We can use apply or specialize to use a hypothesis that is a universal quantification (or implication).

See example below


-- No collisions in the image
def Injective (f : ℝ → ℝ) : Prop := ∀ x y : ℝ, f x = f y → x = y

example (f g : ℝ → ℝ) (hg : Injective g) (hf : Injective f) :
    Injective (g ∘ f) := by {
    unfold Injective at * 
    intro x y h -- The goal is to show P-> Q where P =: f x = f y and Q =: x = y
    -- by intro h we say assume we have P, then we need to show Q
    specialize hf x y 
    specialize hg (f x) (f y) 
    apply hf -- this asks me to now sow that f x = f y  
    apply hg  -- this asks me to show g (f x) = g (f y)
    exact h  -- this is my P
  }

entry.title: TUI Tutorial
entry.content:
How to Build a Terminal User Interface in Rust with Ratatui

A hands-on guide using a real codebase — a research paper manager TUI that searches a SQLite database, displays results in a scrollable list, lets you edit metadata inline, and shells out to vim. Every concept is illustrated with actual code from this project.

Prerequisites: Basic Rust knowledge. No TUI experience needed.

Table of Contents

1. The Mental Model

A TUI app is a loop that redraws the entire screen every frame. There is no persistent widget tree, no DOM, no diffing algorithm you manage. Every iteration:

loop {
    draw_everything_from_scratch();
    read_one_input_event();
    update_state();
}

This is called immediate mode rendering. It's the same pattern used in game engines (Dear ImGui, etc.). It sounds wasteful, but ratatui uses double-buffering internally — it diffs the previous frame against the new one and only sends the changed cells to the terminal. You don't need to think about this.

The architectural pattern this maps to is The Elm Architecture (TEA), also known as Model-View-Update:

              ┌──────────────┐
    Event ──► │    UPDATE     │ ──► State changes
              │  (app.rs)     │
              └──────────────┘
                     │
                     ▼
              ┌──────────────┐
    State ──► │    RENDER     │ ──► Terminal output
              │  (ui.rs)      │
              └──────────────┘
  • State lives in a single App struct. All mutable data in one place.
  • Update is a function that takes an event + current state and produces new state.
  • Render is a function that takes current state and draws the UI. It never mutates state.

This separation is not enforced by ratatui — you could put everything in one file. But keeping update logic (app.rs) separate from rendering (ui.rs) makes the codebase dramatically easier to reason about.

2. Project Setup

Dependencies

# Cargo.toml
[dependencies]
ratatui  = "0.29"     # The TUI framework — widgets, layout, styling
crossterm = "0.28"     # Terminal backend — raw mode, events, colors

Why two crates? Ratatui handles what to draw (widgets, layout). Crossterm handles how to talk to the terminal (escape codes, key events, raw mode). Ratatui supports multiple backends (crossterm, termion, termwiz), but crossterm is the most popular and works on all platforms.

You'll also want whatever crates your app needs. Ours uses:

rusqlite = { version = "0.32", features = ["bundled"] }  # SQLite
toml     = "0.8"                                          # Config files
open     = "5"                                            # Open files in system viewer

File Structure

A clean TUI project splits into four files:

src/
  main.rs      # Terminal setup, main loop, teardown
  app.rs       # App struct, Mode enum, all event handling
  ui.rs        # All rendering (draw functions)
  db.rs        # Data access (database, files, etc.)

This isn't required — you can put everything in main.rs for a toy project. But the moment your app has more than one "screen" or mode, the separation pays for itself immediately.

3. Taking Over the Terminal

A normal terminal does things you don't want in a TUI: it buffers input line-by-line, echoes typed characters, and lets Ctrl+C kill your process. You need to disable all of this and take full control.

// main.rs
use crossterm::{
    execute,
    terminal::{EnterAlternateScreen, LeaveAlternateScreen,
               disable_raw_mode, enable_raw_mode},
};
use ratatui::{Terminal, backend::CrosstermBackend};
use std::io;

fn main() -> io::Result<()> {
    // STEP 1: Enable raw mode.
    //   - Keys are delivered immediately (no waiting for Enter)
    //   - No echo (typed characters don't appear)
    //   - Ctrl+C doesn't kill the process — you get a KeyEvent instead
    enable_raw_mode()?;

    // STEP 2: Enter the alternate screen.
    //   Terminals have two buffers: the "normal" screen (your shell history)
    //   and the "alternate" screen (a blank canvas). TUI apps draw on the
    //   alternate screen. When you leave, the terminal restores the normal
    //   screen — your shell history is untouched.
    let mut stdout = io::stdout();
    execute!(stdout, EnterAlternateScreen)?;

    // STEP 3: Create the ratatui Terminal.
    //   CrosstermBackend adapts crossterm's API to ratatui's Backend trait.
    //   Terminal wraps this and provides draw(), which double-buffers for you.
    let backend = CrosstermBackend::new(stdout);
    let mut terminal = Terminal::new(backend)?;

    // ... run your app ...

    // STEP 4: ALWAYS restore the terminal.
    //   If you skip this (crash, panic, early return), the user's terminal
    //   is stuck in raw mode with no echo. They'll have to type `reset` blind.
    disable_raw_mode()?;
    execute!(terminal.backend_mut(), LeaveAlternateScreen)?;
    terminal.show_cursor()?;

    Ok(())
}

The cardinal rule: always restore the terminal. Structure your code so that teardown runs even if the main loop panics. The pattern from our codebase:

fn main() -> io::Result<()> {
    // setup...
    let result = run_loop(&mut terminal, &mut app);  // might panic/error

    // teardown ALWAYS runs:
    disable_raw_mode()?;
    execute!(terminal.backend_mut(), LeaveAlternateScreen)?;
    terminal.show_cursor()?;

    result  // propagate the error after cleanup
}

4. The Main Loop

The loop is three lines of logic:

fn run_loop(
    terminal: &mut Terminal<CrosstermBackend<io::Stdout>>,
    app: &mut App,
) -> io::Result<()> {
    loop {
        // 1. RENDER: Draw the UI based on current state.
        terminal.draw(|frame| ui::draw(frame, app))?;

        // 2. UPDATE: Read events, modify state.
        app.handle_events()?;

        // 3. CHECK: Should we quit?
        if app.should_quit {
            return Ok(());
        }
    }
}

terminal.draw() takes a closure that receives a Frame. The Frame is your canvas — you render widgets onto it. Ratatui double-buffers: it compares this frame to the previous one and only sends the diff to the terminal. This is why redrawing everything every frame is efficient.

app.handle_events() polls for keyboard/mouse events and updates the App struct. We'll cover this in detail in section 7.

The loop runs at whatever rate events arrive, with a 50ms poll timeout as a floor (~20fps). This is fast enough to feel responsive without burning CPU.

5. Application State — The App Struct

All mutable state lives in one struct. This is the "Model" in Model-View-Update. Here's ours (simplified for teaching):

// app.rs
pub struct App {
    // What mode are we in?
    pub mode: Mode,

    // The data being displayed
    pub papers: Vec<Paper>,
    pub selected: usize,

    // Search state
    pub search_query: String,
    pub search_filter: SearchFilter,

    // Edit state
    pub edit_field: EditField,
    pub editing_active: bool,
    pub edit_paper: Option<Paper>,

    // UI state
    pub status_message: Option<String>,
    pub should_quit: bool,

    // External resources
    pub conn: Connection,         // SQLite
    pub editor_request: Option<PathBuf>,  // request to open vim
}

Why one big struct? Because the render function needs to see everything to draw the UI, and the update function needs to modify anything in response to input. Splitting state across multiple structs creates borrow checker pain with no architectural benefit.

Initialization loads data from the database:

impl App {
    pub fn new(conn: Connection) -> Self {
        let papers = db::list_all(&conn);
        Self {
            mode: Mode::Browse,
            papers,
            selected: 0,
            search_query: String::new(),
            // ... all other fields initialized to defaults ...
            conn,
        }
    }
}

6. Modes — How TUIs Handle Context

A TUI can't show modal dialogs the way a GUI can. Instead, it uses modes — different interpretations of the same keys depending on context. Think vim: pressing j in Normal mode moves down, but in Insert mode it types the letter "j".

#[derive(Debug, Clone, Copy, PartialEq)]
pub enum Mode {
    Browse,  // Navigating the list. j/k move, Enter opens, q quits.
    Search,  // Typing into the search box. Characters are input.
    Edit,    // Editing metadata. Navigate fields, type values.
}

Modes affect two things:

  1. Key handling — the same key does different things in different modes.
  2. Rendering — the UI changes visually to show which mode you're in (highlighted borders, different status bar text, etc.).

The mode is just a field on the App struct. Switching modes is a simple assignment:

// Enter search mode when the user presses '/'
KeyCode::Char('/') => {
    self.mode = Mode::Search;
}

// Leave search mode when they press Escape
KeyCode::Esc => {
    self.mode = Mode::Browse;
}

Design tip: Keep mode transitions explicit and obvious. The user should always know what mode they're in. Use visual cues: change border colors, show mode-specific keybindings in the status bar, show/hide cursor indicators.

7. Handling Keyboard Input

Event handling is the UPDATE step. We poll for events, dispatch by mode, and modify state:

pub fn handle_events(&mut self) -> std::io::Result<()> {
    // Poll with 50ms timeout. If no event arrives, we return and re-render.
    // This timeout controls your "frame rate" when idle.
    if event::poll(Duration::from_millis(50))? {
        if let Event::Key(key) = event::read()? {
            match self.mode {
                Mode::Browse => self.handle_browse_key(key),
                Mode::Search => self.handle_search_key(key),
                Mode::Edit   => self.handle_edit_key(key),
            }
        }
    }
    Ok(())
}

Each mode gets its own handler. Here's Browse mode:

fn handle_browse_key(&mut self, key: KeyEvent) {
    match key.code {
        KeyCode::Char('q') => self.should_quit = true,

        // Navigation: support both arrow keys and vim keys
        KeyCode::Down | KeyCode::Char('j') => {
            if !self.papers.is_empty() {
                self.selected = (self.selected + 1).min(self.papers.len() - 1);
            }
        }
        KeyCode::Up | KeyCode::Char('k') => {
            self.selected = self.selected.saturating_sub(1);
        }

        // Mode transitions
        KeyCode::Char('/') => self.mode = Mode::Search,
        KeyCode::Char('e') => self.enter_edit_mode(),
        KeyCode::Enter     => self.open_selected_pdf(),

        _ => {}
    }
}

Navigation pattern: Use min() and saturating_sub() to clamp the selection index. Never let it go negative or past the end. This is a bug in almost every TUI tutorial — they forget to bounds-check.

Search mode treats most keys as text input:

fn handle_search_key(&mut self, key: KeyEvent) {
    match key.code {
        KeyCode::Esc       => self.mode = Mode::Browse,
        KeyCode::Enter     => self.mode = Mode::Browse,
        KeyCode::Backspace => { self.search_query.pop(); self.refresh_search(); }
        KeyCode::Char(c)   => { self.search_query.push(c); self.refresh_search(); }
        KeyCode::Tab       => { self.search_filter = self.search_filter.next();
                                self.refresh_search(); }
        _ => {}
    }
}

Notice refresh_search() is called on every keystroke — this is what makes search results update live.

Modifier keys (Ctrl, Alt, Shift) are checked via the modifiers field on KeyEvent:

KeyCode::Char('s') if key.modifiers.contains(KeyModifiers::CONTROL) => {
    self.save_edit();
}

8. The Layout System — Dividing the Screen

Ratatui's Layout splits a Rect (a rectangle: x, y, width, height) into smaller Rects. You compose layouts vertically and horizontally to create your screen structure.

//   ┌──────────────────────────────┐
//   │ Search bar          (3 rows) │  ← Constraint::Length(3)
//   ├──────────────────────────────┤
//   │                              │
//   │ Paper list        (flexible) │  ← Constraint::Fill(1)
//   │                              │
//   ├──────────────────────────────┤
//   │ Detail panel        (8 rows) │  ← Constraint::Length(8)
//   ├──────────────────────────────┤
//   │ Status bar          (1 row)  │  ← Constraint::Length(1)
//   └──────────────────────────────┘

let layout = Layout::vertical([
    Constraint::Length(3),   // Search bar: exactly 3 rows
    Constraint::Fill(1),     // Paper list: all remaining space
    Constraint::Length(8),   // Detail panel: exactly 8 rows
    Constraint::Length(1),   // Status bar: exactly 1 row
])
.split(frame.area());

// layout[0], layout[1], layout[2], layout[3] are now Rects
// you can pass to widget rendering functions.
draw_search_bar(frame, app, layout[0]);
draw_paper_list(frame, app, layout[1]);
draw_detail_panel(frame, app, layout[2]);
draw_status_bar(frame, app, layout[3]);

Constraint Types

ConstraintBehavior
Length(n)Exactly n rows/columns. Use for fixed-size elements.
Min(n)At least n, but can grow.
Max(n)At most n.
Percentage(n)n% of the parent.
Fill(weight)Takes remaining space. Multiple Fills share proportionally by weight.

Nesting layouts: You can split horizontally inside a vertical section. For example, to put a search box and a filter selector side by side:

let row = Layout::horizontal([
    Constraint::Fill(1),      // Search box takes most space
    Constraint::Length(10),   // Filter selector is fixed width
])
.split(layout[0]);

Key insight: Layouts are computed, not stored. You call split() every frame, which returns fresh Rects. This means your layout automatically adapts when the terminal is resized — no resize event handling needed.

9. Rendering Widgets

Ratatui provides built-in widgets. The most important ones:

WidgetUse case
BlockBorders, titles, background colors. Wraps other widgets.
ParagraphText display. Supports styled spans, wrapping, alignment.
ListScrollable list with selection.
TableTabular data with columns.
GaugeProgress bars.
TabsTab selector.

Rendering a widget is a single call:

frame.render_widget(some_widget, some_rect);

The widget draws itself into the given Rect. That's it.

Block — The Universal Container

Almost every element starts with a Block. It draws borders, a title, background color, and padding. Then you render your content into the Block's inner area:

let block = Block::default()
    .borders(Borders::ALL)
    .border_style(Style::default().fg(BORDER))
    .title(" Details ")
    .style(Style::default().bg(BG_SECONDARY))
    .padding(Padding::horizontal(1));

// block.inner(area) returns the Rect INSIDE the borders and padding.
let inner = block.inner(area);
frame.render_widget(block, area);

// Now render content into the inner area.
frame.render_widget(Paragraph::new("Hello"), inner);

Important: Render the Block first, then your content. The Block fills its area with the background color. If you render content first, the Block overwrites it.

Paragraph — Styled Text

Paragraph renders text with rich styling. The key concept is Spans and Lines:

  • A Span is a styled piece of text: Span::styled("hello", Style::default().fg(Color::Red))
  • A Line is a sequence of Spans (one row of text)
  • A Paragraph is a sequence of Lines
let line = Line::from(vec![
    Span::styled("Title: ", Style::default().fg(TEXT_SECONDARY).bold()),
    Span::styled("Attention Is All You Need", Style::default().fg(TEXT_PRIMARY)),
]);
frame.render_widget(Paragraph::new(line), area);

This is how you get mixed styling on a single line — each Span has its own colors and modifiers.

10. Styling — Colors, Borders, and Themes

Every visual element in ratatui is controlled by Style. A Style has:

  • fg — foreground (text) color
  • bg — background color
  • Modifiers: BOLD, ITALIC, UNDERLINED, DIM, etc.
Style::default()
    .fg(Color::Rgb(124, 111, 239))  // Purple accent
    .bg(Color::Rgb(30, 30, 46))     // Dark background
    .add_modifier(Modifier::BOLD)

Defining a Color Palette

Define your colors as constants so they're consistent everywhere:

// Catppuccin-inspired dark theme
const BG_PRIMARY: Color   = Color::Rgb(30, 30, 46);      // #1e1e2e
const BG_SECONDARY: Color = Color::Rgb(37, 37, 54);      // #252536
const BG_INPUT: Color     = Color::Rgb(42, 42, 60);      // #2a2a3c
const BORDER: Color       = Color::Rgb(58, 58, 78);      // #3a3a4e
const ACCENT: Color       = Color::Rgb(124, 111, 239);   // #7c6fef
const TEXT_PRIMARY: Color  = Color::Rgb(224, 222, 244);   // #e0def4
